set.st: About 1849 ('about 25 years' before 1874) John McArdill, a jewellery pedlar from London, Canada, was robbed of $4,000-5,000 in coin, watches and jewellery. A deathbed letter from the thief, dated 12 Sep 1873 and postmarked Branch County, said the loot was in a dry well on the south side of the Kalamazoo River in the Newbre neighbourhood, at a stated distance from the old graveyard and about eighty paces from the road, the well filled with oak stumps. The well was found on N. A. Burton's lot as described. On 10 Sep 1874 McArdill's diggers hit the stumps about 40 ft down, and on 24 Sep the Detroit News reported that he 'has got to the bottom of his well at last, and has found no treasure … a disappointed and disgusted man.' The Free Press of the same day says six men had widened the well to 10 ft and the work was given up on 22 Sep 1874 after about $200 was spent; its theories were that the other robber had already taken the money, that the letter was cooked up on a medium's advice, or that it was a grudge hoax. By late October 'the belief has become almost universal' that McArdill got the money on the last day: a neighbour said the diggers had not reached bottom when he went to dinner and were hastily filling the hole when he came back. Pin is the half-mile stake the letter paced from, not the well itself. The Free Press of 15 Sep 1874 adds that the well had been filled 12-14 years earlier and cropped over, and that the diggers were McArdill and his son, the well-digger Joe Jackson and three labourers.

src: Detroit Free Press, 24 Sep 1874, p. 1, Battle Creek column (Newspapers.com 1048530708)
